content: Vision loss refers to the reduction or complete absence of vision. Blindness is defined as a lack of vision, which may also include vision loss that cannot be corrected with glasses or contact lenses. Partial blindness indicates severely limited vision, while complete blindness means the inability to see anything, including light. Most people who use the term blindness are referring to complete blindness. In the United States, individuals with vision worse than 20/200 are considered legally blind in most states. Vision loss can occur suddenly or gradually over time, and not all types of vision loss result in complete blindness. Causes of Vision Loss Blindness can result from various causes. In the United States, the leading causes include: Accidents or injuries to the eye's surface, such as chemical burns or sports-related injuries. Diabetes, which can lead to blurred vision, shadows, missing areas in the visual field, and difficulty seeing at night. Glaucoma, which may cause tunnel vision and blurry vision. Macular degeneration, where central vision is progressively lost while peripheral vision remains intact. Other causes of vision loss include: Blocked blood vessels in the eye. Complications from premature birth, such as retrolental fibroplasia. Complications following eye surgery. Amblyopia (lazy eye). Optic neuritis (inflammation of the optic nerve). Stroke. Retinitis pigmentosa (a genetic disorder affecting the retina). Tumors, such as retinoblastoma or optic glioma. When to Seek Urgent Medical Care Sudden vision loss is always a medical emergency, even if it is not complete. It should never be ignored or assumed to improve on its own. Immediate consultation with an ophthalmologist or a visit to the emergency room is essential. Most serious forms of vision loss are painless, but the absence of pain does not reduce the urgency of seeking medical attention. Many types of vision loss have a limited window for successful treatment. Diagnosis A comprehensive eye examination will be conducted to determine the cause of vision loss. Treatment will depend on the underlying cause. For individuals with long-term vision loss, consulting a low-vision specialist can provide guidance on self-care and maintaining a fulfilling life. Treatment Options Home Care The type of home assistance required depends on the nature of the vision loss. It is crucial for individuals with blindness to maintain independence in dressing, eating, and ensuring safety. Numerous services are available to provide training and support for independent living. Organizational Tips for the Home: Keep specific items in designated drawers, cabinets, or counter spaces. Learn to identify items by their shape, such as egg cartons or cereal boxes. Use plastic rings to keep pairs of socks together during washing, drying, and storage. Label items with small Braille labels or raised dots, rubber bands, Velcro, or colored tape. Mark appliance settings (e.g., on, bake, or temperature settings) with raised dots, caulking, or rubber markers. Use phones with large numbers and memorize the keypad layout. Fold different denominations of paper money in distinct ways (e.g., fold a $10 bill in half or double-fold a $20 bill). Use Braille or large-print checks. Safety Tips for Navigation and Home Environment: Learn to use a long white cane for independent mobility. When walking with assistance, hold the helper's arm above the elbow and walk slightly behind them to follow their movements. Remove loose wires or cords from the floor. Eliminate loose throw rugs. Avoid keeping small pets in the home. Repair uneven flooring in doorways. Ensure adequate lighting throughout the home. Install handrails in the bathtub, shower, and near the toilet. Use slip-proof mats in the bathtub or shower. Low-Vision Aids: Magnifiers. Technological aids to facilitate the use of cell phones and computers. Watches designed for individuals with low vision, as well as talking watches and clocks. Where to Find Medical Care for Vision Loss Individuals experiencing vision loss should seek care from an ophthalmologist or a specialized medical professional. Early diagnosis and treatment are critical to managing vision loss effectively.
